notes.short: Darkness, a cloud, blackness: one wish, three times
notes.about: Each line asks the same thing in other words: let darkness cover the day of Job's birth. Darkness and gloom, a cloud, and the blackness of the day answer one another, and so the word for blackness can be read as whatever darkens a day.

lines.words: May darkness and gloom reclaim it,
and a cloud settle over it;
may the blackness of the day overwhelm it.

original.note: In Hebrew the word for blackness is found only here; it is read from a verb for being black or dark.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes reads the word for blackness as obscurations, whatever darkens the day, because that sense suits the parallel lines, and sets aside a reading of it as a scorching desert wind, which does not suit them: Job wished all that makes a day gloomy to rest on it. He notes that the noun is found only here, but that its verb is used of being black and dark.
notes.limit: Scholars differ on the word for blackness: some take it as scorching heat or as bitterness.

cites.quote: But this interpretation does not well suit the parallelism. Others, therefore, understand by the word, "obscurations," or whatever darkens the day. ... The noun here is not found elsewhere; but the "verb" כמר kâmar is used in the sense of being black and dark ... This meaning suits the parallelism ... Job wished that everything which could render the day gloomy and obscure might rest upon it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The hungry eat, the thirsty pant: his goods are gone
notes.about: The last line says the first again in other words. The hungry who consume his harvest are answered by the thirsty who pant after his wealth: what the fool gathered is eaten and drunk up by others.

lines.words: The hungry consume his harvest,
and the thirsty pant after his wealth.

notes.evidence: A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the word should be read as the thirsty, since the hungry of the parallel line proves it. Adam Clarke reads it the same way, as set against the hungry of the earlier clause: the hungry eat up the grain and the thirsty drink down the wine and oil.
notes.limit: Scholars differ on one Hebrew word in the last line: many read it as the thirsty, as the BSB does, and others as a snare or a schemer.

cites.quote: the robber--as the Sabeans, who robbed Job. Rather, translate "the thirsty," as the antithesis in the parallelism, "the hungry," proves.

cites.quote: Or, more properly, the thirsty, צמים tsammim, as is plain from their swallowing up or gulping down; opposed to the hungry or half-starved, mentioned in the preceding clause. The hungry shall eat up their grain, and the thirsty shall drink down their wine and oil

notes.short: Job's friends as the only wise men: said in irony
notes.about: Job seems to grant that his friends are the only wise people, so that wisdom will die with them. He means the opposite, as the next verse says: “I am not inferior to you.” Their speeches had told him nothing he did not know.

figure.name: Irony
figure.words: you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die
figure.means: that his friends were no wiser than he was, for all their claim to teach him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under irony spoken by men: Job's friends had no more knowledge than he. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the words are meant as irony, as if all understanding were theirs alone. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls them ironical, Clarke a strong irony, and Henry says Job speaks ironically of their claim to all wisdom.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Human Irony, p. 813
cites.quote: This powerful Irony is meant to emphasise the fact that Job’s friends had no more knowledge than he

cites.quote: Doubtless ye are the wisest men in the world; all wisdom is concentrated in you; and when ye die, there will no more be found on the face of the earth! This is a strong irony.

notes.short: Night, then morning; then back to the night
notes.about: Verse 19 can be read as the wicked man's sudden end, either in the night after he lies down, or by day after he opens his eyes. Verse 20 then answers the two crosswise: first terrors like a flood, then a tempest in the night, so the night opens and closes the picture.

lines.words: He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more;
when he opens his eyes, all is gone.
Terrors overtake him like a flood;
a tempest sweeps him away in the night.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) reads verse 19 as sudden death, either in the night after the man lies down rich or by day after he opens his eyes in the morning, and says the two lines of verse 20 are attached crosswise to that picture of destruction by night or by day: the terrors of death seize him like a flood, and by night a whirlwind carries him away.
notes.limit: The first line of verse 20 names no time; it answers the day only by its place in the crossing. Other writers take lying down in verse 19 as dying, not as going to bed, and do not mark this order.

cites.quote: he lieth down to sleep rich, and he doeth it no more, since in the night he is removed from life ... by sudden death; or also: in the morning he openeth his eyes ... he closes them for ever ... attached crosswise (chiastisch) to this picture of sudden destruction, be it by night or by day: the terrors of death seize him ... like a flood ... by night a whirlwind ... carrieth him away
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The realm of the dead speaks of wisdom
notes.about: Abaddon and Death, the world of the dead, are made to speak like persons, as the ocean depths do in verse 14. Even there wisdom is known only by a rumor: they have heard of it, but they do not understand it.

figure.name: Personification
figure.means: the world of the dead, which has only heard a distant report of wisdom

original.note: In Hebrew Abaddon means destruction; here, as in Job 26:6, it names the world of the dead.

notes.evidence: Barnes calls the verse a personification, and an exceedingly sublime one; he takes Abaddon, as in Job 26:6, for the world of the dead, whose deep and dark regions had only heard a distant report of wisdom and did not understand it.

cites.quote: Destruction - This is a personification which is exceedingly sublime. ... see the notes at Job 26:6. It is employed here, as in that place, to denote the nether world - the abode of departed spirits ... The sense is, that those deep and dark regions had simply heard the distant report of wisdom but they did not understand it

notes.short: Six troubles, even seven: however many come
notes.about: Eliphaz tells Job that God will rescue him from six calamities, then raises the count to seven. The numbers do not count troubles: they mean that however many come, God is able to deliver from them all.

figure.name: Numerical saying
figure.words: six calamities; no harm will touch you in seven
figure.means: every trouble that may come, however many

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes (Barnes' Notes) says six is an indefinite number, one more added to mean every case. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a number, then the next higher, for all possible troubles. Clarke: six and seven are put for many. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): formed like the number proverbs, still more than six. Henry: however often troubles come, God delivers out of them all.
notes.limit: These are Eliphaz's words to Job. The note is on how he counts, not on whether his counsel fit Job's case.

cites.quote: Six is used here to denote an indefinite number, meaning that he would support in many troubles. This mode of speech is not uncommon among the Hebrews, where one number is mentioned, so that an extreme number may be immediately added. The method is, to mention a number within the limit, and then to add one more, meaning that in all instances the thing referred to would occur.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Hebrew idiom fixes on a certain number (here "six"), in order to call attention as to a thing of importance; then increases the force by adding, with a "yea, nay seven," the next higher number; here "seven," the sacred and perfect number. In all possible troubles; not merely in the precise number "seven."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The numbers six and seven are put here for many. Though a number of troubles should come upon thee all at once, and there should be no hope, humanly speaking, yet God would rid thee out of them all

cites.quote: Job 5:19 is formed after the manner of the so-called number-proverbs ... in six troubles, yea in still more than six.

notes.short: Job's friends fail him like streams that run dry
notes.about: Job says his friends have failed him like desert streams, swollen with ice and snow in winter but gone in the summer heat. The caravans of Tema and Sheba come looking for water and are confounded. So his friends, who came to comfort him, have given him no help.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: my brothers are as faithless as wadis
figure.means: Job's friends, who seemed to promise much comfort and gave none, as streams full in winter fail thirsty travelers in summer

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls the similitude very elegant: the friends' show is the swollen brook, and Job's hope the thirsty traveler's. Albert Barnes calls the simile exquisitely beautiful, Job's hope for comfort like travelers' hope of water. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says Job compares his friends to the swollen wady. Adam Clarke says Job compares them to torrents that soon pass away.
notes.limit: These writers read verse 18 of the streams themselves, wandering from their channels until they come to nothing; the BSB reads it of caravans that turn aside from their routes.

cites.quote: This disappointment which Job met with he here illustrates by the failing of brooks in summer. 1. The similitude is very elegant ... (1.) Their pretensions are fitly compared to the great show which the brooks make when they are swollen with the waters of a land flood
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: I looked for the language of condolence and compassion; for something to cheer my heart, and to uphold me in my trials - as weary and thirsty travelers look for water and are sadly disappointed when they come to the place where they expected to find it, and find the stream dried up. The simile used here is exquisitely beautiful
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Job compares his friends to the wady swollen by ice and snow water, and even to the travelling bands themselves languishing for water. He thirsts for friendly solace, but the seeming comfort which his friends utter is only as the scattered meandering waters in which the mountain brook leaks out.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The approach of Job's friends promised much of sympathy and compassion; his expectations were raised: but their conduct soon convinced him that they were physicians of no value; therefore he compares them to the deceitful torrents that soon pass away.

notes.short: Job longs for rest like a hired man for evening
notes.about: Job asks whether man's days on earth are not like a hired hand's. A slave longs for the evening shade and a hireling waits for his wages; so Job is allotted months of futility and nights of misery. The point left unsaid is read as Job longing for death as rest after toil.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Like a slave he longs for shade
figure.means: Job himself, who longs for death as rest after hard labor, as a worn-out worker longs for evening and his pay

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls the comparison plain: as a tired servant wishes for evening, so Job wishes for death; Albert Barnes says so too. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the point is that Job waits for death as rest after hard labor. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) asks why, if the servant longs for evening, Job may not long for his hard service to close.
notes.limit: Two of these writers hear in the hireling's wages Job's hope of a reward after this life; the others speak only of rest from toil.

cites.quote: He had as much reason, he thought, to wish for death, as a poor servant or hireling that is tired with his work has to wish for the shadows of the evening, when he shall receive his penny and go to rest ... The comparison is plain, the application is concise and somewhat obscure, but we must supply a word or two, and then it is easy
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The meaning of Job is, that as a servant looked impatiently for the shades of the evening when he would be dismissed from toil, so he longed for death. And as an hireling looketh - That is, he anxiously desires his work to be finished, and expects the reward of his labors. So Job looked to the reward of a life of toil and piety.

cites.quote: The conclusion is intended to be: thus I wait for death as refreshing and rest after hard labour. He goes, however, beyond this next point of comparison, or rather he remains on this side of it.

notes.short: The godless wither like papyrus without water
notes.about: Bildad asks whether papyrus can grow without a marsh, or reeds without water. Without water, they dry up while still green and uncut, quicker than grass. “Such is the destiny of all who forget God”: the godless may flourish for a time, but their hope has no lasting ground and soon perishes.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Such is the destiny of all who forget God
figure.means: the godless, who flourish for a time on ground that cannot last, then wither suddenly, like papyrus cut off from water

notes.evidence: Henry says the hypocrite's hopes are here compared to a rush or flag, which withers before any other herb. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) gives two points of likeness: lush growth, then sudden ruin. Barnes says those who forget God are like the paper-reed, seeming to flourish with nothing firm; Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch), that Bildad likens the false ground of their prosperity to it.
notes.limit: These are Bildad's words to Job. The note is on the likeness he draws, not on whether it fit Job's case.

cites.quote: He illustrates this truth by some similitudes. 1. The hopes and joys of the hypocrite are here compared to a rush or flag, ... It withers presently, before any other herb ... The hope of hypocrites is a great cheat upon themselves, and, though it may flourish for a while, it will certainly perish at last, and they with it.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Job 8:11-13 embody in poetic and sententious form (probably the fragment of an old poem) the observation of the elders. The double point of comparison between the ungodly and the paper-reed is: 1. the luxuriant prosperity at first; and, 2. the sudden destruction.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: They who forget God are like the paper-reed. They seem to flourish, but they have nothing that is firm and substantial. As the paper-reed soon dies, as the flag withers away before any other herb, so it will be with the wicked, though apparently prosperous.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Bildad likens the deceitful ground on which the prosperity of the godless stands to the dry ground on which, only for a time, the papyrus or reed finds water, and grows up rapidly: shooting up quickly, it withers as quickly

notes.short: The godless man as a lush plant torn up
notes.about: Bildad pictures the godless man as a well-watered plant in the sunshine. Its shoots spread over the garden and its roots wrap around the stones, yet once it is uprooted, its place disowns it: “I never saw you.” He thinks his prosperity secure, but it ends suddenly, and others spring up in his place.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: He is a well-watered plant in the sunshine
figure.means: the godless man in his prosperity: spreading and seemingly secure, yet soon torn up and forgotten

notes.evidence: Henry says the hypocrite is here compared to a flourishing, well-rooted tree that is easily cut down. Barnes calls it a new illustration comparing the hypocrite with a quick-growing plant that withers; Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the ungodly man is likened to a creeping plant throughout; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), that as the soil disowns the withered weeds, friends disown him.
notes.limit: Writers differ on the kind of plant: a well-rooted tree, a quick-growing plant without depth of root, or a creeper or weeds over stones. These are Bildad's words to Job; the note is on his picture, not on whether it fit Job's case.

cites.quote: The hypocrite is here compared to a flourishing and well-rooted tree, which, though it do not wither of itself, yet will easily be cut down and its place know it no more. ... Thus does a wicked man, when he prospers in the world, think himself secure; his wealth is a high wall in his own conceit.

notes.short: Roots round the rock heap, a home among stones
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: the plant's roots wrap around the rock heap, and it looks for a home among the stones. Read side by side, the heap is a pile of stones, and the wicked man is pictured as a plant growing among rocks.

lines.words: His roots wrap around the rock heap;
he looks for a home among the stones.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes says the word for heap means either a heap of stones or a spring, that the parallelism demands its usual sense here, and that the wicked man is like a plant standing among rocks, rubbish or old ruins, not in fertile soil.
notes.limit: Scholars differ on the word for heap: some read it as a spring, and take the verse as the roots of a well-watered plant.

cites.quote: The word גל gal, rendered "heap," means either (1.) A heap, as a heap of stones ... (2.) A fountain or spring ... The parallelism, if nothing else, demands that the usual signification should be given to it here; and the true sense is, that the prosperous wicked man or the hypocrite is like a plant which stands in the midst of rocks, rubbish, or old ruins

notes.short: Power to the wicked, the judges' faces covered
notes.about: The second line sets the judges against the wicked of the first. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked, while the judges, read as the upright who are fit to judge, have their faces covered: kept out of sight, or led away as condemned men.

lines.words: The earth is given into the hand of the wicked;
He blindfolds its judges.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes says the parallel lines require the judges to be the righteous, kept in obscurity while the wicked rule the earth. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) sets the righteous judges against the wicked of the first line and says they are led to execution with faces covered. Matthew Henry: God advances the wicked while the wise and good are buried in obscurity.
notes.limit: Scholars differ on the second line: some read it as the judges blinded, so that they judge unjustly, which makes both lines tell of the same wrong.

cites.quote: The parallelism requires us to understand it as meaning that while the wicked had dominion over the earth, the righteous were in obscurity, or were not advanced to honor and power. The word "judges," therefore, I think, is to be understood of the righteous judges, of those who are qualified to administer justice. Their face is covered. They are kept in concealment.

notes.short: Washed with snow, cleansed with lye
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: washing with snow is answered by cleansing the hands with lye, each line naming a thing that cleanses. Yet, as the next verse says, God would still plunge him into the pit.

lines.words: If I should wash myself with snow
and cleanse my hands with lye,

notes.short: Unlike a tree, man is like water that dries up
notes.about: Job sets a man beside a tree. A stump that is cut down can sprout again at the scent of water, “But a man dies and is laid low.” Then he likens a man's death to water that disappears from the sea and a river that dries up: so a man lies down and does not rise.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: As water disappears from the sea
figure.means: a man's death: like water dried up from its bed, he passes from this life and does not come back to it

notes.evidence: Barnes says that as the waters vanish and leave the bed dry, so man passes away and leaves nothing; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), that the dry channel answers to the body laid out in death. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says this vanishing is set under the figure of water that dries up; Henry, that man will not revive as a tree does, and his life may be compared to a land-flood.
notes.limit: Many read the verses as speaking of a return to this life on earth, not as a denial of life to come; verses 13 to 15 go on to hope.

cites.quote: As the waters evaporate wholly, and leave the bottom wholly dry, so it is with man, who passes entirely away, and leaves nothing. ... As such torrents vanish wholly away, so it was with man. Every vestige disappeared

notes.short: Corruption his father, the worm his mother
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. Job calls corruption his father, then the worm his mother or his sister: in both lines he names the decay of the grave as his nearest kin, so close does death seem to him.

lines.words: and say to corruption, ‘You are my father,’
and to the worm, ‘My mother,’ or ‘My sister,’

original.note: In Hebrew the word for worm is feminine, and it is the one called mother and sister; corruption, called father, answers it in the first line.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes takes the first line's word as corruption, which he says fits the other half of the verse and answers the worm better than grave would, and says Job is as near to the worms as a son to his mother. Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the feminine worm is addressed as mother and sister, so father has a masculine object, corruption: Job is bound to both by the closest ties.
notes.limit: The first line's word can also mean the pit or the grave; here it is read as corruption, as the BSB has it.

cites.quote: This accords, certainly, with the other hemistich, and better constitutes a parallelism with the "worm" than the word "grave" would. It seems probable that this is the sense here ... My mother - I am so nearly allied to the worms, that the connection may be compared to that between a mother and her son.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: To corruption and the worm he already cries, father! and, mother! sister! ... and the stars are not pure in His sight,

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes takes the first line to mean one and the same Creator, and says the Hebrew of the second line will bear another reading, but the parallel rather requires the One to be that same Maker. Either way, he says, they had a common origin and equal rights.
notes.limit: The Hebrew of the second line can also be read as fashioned in one womb. Either way, master and servant share one origin.

cites.quote: Had we not one and the same Creator ... did he not fashion us in one womb? The Hebrew will bear either construction, but the parallelism rather requires that given in the text ... The sentiment is, whichever interpretation be adopted, that they had a common origin; that God would watch over them alike as his children; and that, therefore, they had equal rights.

notes.short: The sun's radiance, then the moon's splendor
notes.about: The two lines are built alike, each naming a light of the sky and how it shines: the sun in its radiance, then the moon moving in splendor. Job speaks of beholding them as objects of worship, as verse 27 goes on to show.

lines.words: if I have beheld the sun in its radiance
or the moon moving in splendor,

original.note: In Hebrew the first line has or, “light”, which here means the sun, set beside yareach, “moon”, in the second.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the Hebrew word for light here means the sun, as the moon stands in the parallel member, and that Job refers to idolatrous worship. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) also takes light as the sun, and says the moon's majestic course answers to the sun's shooting forth rays, both being what Job saw.

cites.quote: The Hebrew word (אור 'ôr) properly means light, but that it here means the sun is manifest from the connection, since the moon occurs in the parallel member of the sentence. ... There is no doubt that Job here refers to idolatrous worship
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: אור is here, as Job 37:21 and φάος in Homer, the sun as the great light of the earth. ... The two words יקר הלד describe with exceeding beauty the solemn majestic wandering of the moon; יקר is acc. of closer definition, like תמים, Psa 15:2 , and this "brilliantly rolling on" is the acc. of the predicate to אראה, corresponding to the כּי יחל, "that (or how) it shoots forth rays"
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Land and tenants frame the furrows and produce
notes.about: The four lines turn back on themselves. The first and last go together: the land crying out against Job, and its tenants broken in spirit. The middle two go together too: the weeping furrows and the produce eaten without payment, which can be read of workers unpaid for tilling and for the harvest.

lines.words: if my land cries out against me
and its furrows weep together,
if I have devoured its produce without payment
or broken the spirit of its tenants,

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says that of the four clauses in verses 38 and 39, the first refers to the same subject as the fourth, and the second is joined to the third by introverted parallelism. He takes the furrows as likely pointing to the laborer unpaid for tilling, and the eaten produce to the laborer unpaid for gathering the harvest.
notes.limit: The pairing of the middle lines rests on reading both of workers left unpaid; the four lines can also be read together as one charge of wrong done to the land's owners.

cites.quote: furrows--The specification of these makes it likely, he implies in this, "If I paid not the laborer for tillage"; as Job 31:39 , "If I paid him not for gathering in the fruits." Thus of the four clauses in Job 31:38-39 , the first refers to the same subject as the fourth, the second is connected with the third by introverted parallelism.

notes.short: A spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty
notes.about: The second line can be read as saying the first again in other words: the spirit in a man is the breath of the Almighty, and it is this that gives understanding. So wisdom is God's gift, not a matter of years, and young Elihu may speak.

lines.words: But there is a spirit in a man,
the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding.

original.note: In Hebrew the lines pair ruach, “spirit”, with neshamah, “breath”: the spirit in man is breathed into him by God.

notes.evidence: Barnes says the spirit in man is one imparted from the Almighty, as the parallelism seems to require, since it answers to the inspiration of the Almighty in the other half, and that wisdom is God's gift and may be found in a youth. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) takes the halves not as opposed but as a synonymous or progressive parallelism, man's spirit being breathed into him by God's Spirit.
notes.limit: The second line may also be read as carrying the thought further, naming the breath of the Almighty as what gives understanding.

cites.quote: This evidently refers to a spirit imparted from above; a spirit from the Almighty. The parallelism seems to require this, for it responds to the phrase "the inspiration of the Almighty" in the other hemistich. ... He now finds that wisdom is not the attribute of rank or station, but that it is the gift of God, and therefore it may be found in a youth.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The two halves of the verse are, on the contrary, a synonymous ("the spirit, it is in man, viz., that is and acts") or progressive parallelism ... the spirit of man is the principle of life creatively wrought, and indeed breathed into him, by the Spirit of God
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Honest words, from one perfect in knowledge
notes.about: The second line can be read as saying the first again from another side. Elihu's words are free of falsehood, and the one Job has to deal with is a man of integrity in his views, unlike the friends, who defended God with unsound arguments.

lines.words: For truly my words are free of falsehood;
one perfect in knowledge is with you.

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) renders the second line, as the parallelism requires, of a man of integrity in his views: Elihu means himself, who will not vindicate God by unsound arguments as the friends did.
notes.limit: Others read the second line of Elihu's clear understanding rather than his honesty, or of God, who is called perfect in knowledge in Job 37:16.

cites.quote: I will not "speak wickedly for God," as the friends ( Job 13:4 , Job 13:7-8 ) --that is, vindicate God by unsound arguments. he that is perfect, &c.--Rather, as the parallelism requires, "a man of integrity in sentiments is with thee" (is he with whom thou hast to do). Elihu means himself, as opposed to the dishonest reasonings of the friends
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Dying young, like the shrine prostitutes
notes.about: The second line says the first again. They die in their youth, and their life ends as the lives of the male shrine prostitutes end, early and in shame. This is the end of the godless of verse 13, who do not cry for help when God binds them.

lines.words: They die in their youth,
among the male shrine prostitutes.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line says their soul (nefesh) dies in youth, and the second answers with their life (chayyah) among the shrine prostitutes.

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) reads the second line as their life ended like that of the unclean, early and in dishonor, so that it answers to the first. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says the word for life in the second line interchanges with the word for soul in the first, and takes their life as like that of the shrine prostitutes, worn out before their time.

cites.quote: Rather ( Deu 23:17 ), Their life is (ended) as that of (literally, "among") the unclean, prematurely and dishonorably. So the second clause answers to the first.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Thus their soul dieth in the vigour of youth, And their life is like that of the unclean. ... חיּה interchanges with נפשׁ, as Job 33:22 , Job 33:28 ... are the consecrated men, who yielded themselves up, like the women in honour of the deity, to passive, prematurely-enervating incontinence
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Two ways God clears away the storm clouds
notes.about: The two lines answer each other. In the first God loads the clouds with water until they fall as rain; in the second He scatters the clouds that carry His lightning. Either way the storm passes and the sky is left clear.

lines.words: He loads the clouds with moisture;
He scatters His lightning through them.

original.note: In Hebrew the first verb means He burdens the clouds, and the second line reads, He scatters the cloud of His light, that is, the cloud of His lightning.

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the first verb, God burdening the cloud so that it falls in rain, answers to the parallel verb scatters, a clear sky coming alike from both. The cloud scattered is literally the cloud of His light, that is, of His lightning. A rendering of the first line as brightness driving the clouds away suits the parallel, he says, but the Hebrew hardly allows it.
notes.limit: Some render the first line of brightness driving the clouds away; that suits the parallel too, but the Hebrew hardly allows it.

cites.quote: wearieth--burdeneth it, so that it falls in rain; thus "wearieth" answers to the parallel "scattereth" ... a clear sky resulting alike from both. bright cloud--literally, "cloud of his light," that is, of His lightning. UMBREIT ... translates; "Brightness drives away the clouds, His light scattereth the thick clouds"; the parallelism is thus good, but the Hebrew hardly sanctions it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Sun, wind, north, majesty: lines that turn back
notes.about: The lines go out and come back in reverse order. No one can gaze at the bright sun, and the wind sweeps the skies clean; then golden splendor comes out of the north, perhaps the quarter of the clearing wind, and awesome majesty surrounds God, answering the sun too bright to look at.

lines.words: Now no one can gaze at the sun when it is bright in the skies
after the wind has swept them clean.
Out of the north He comes in golden splendor;
awesome majesty surrounds Him.

notes.evidence: Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it inverted parallelism: the first clause of verse 22, out of the north, answers to the last clause of verse 21, perhaps because the north wind clears the air, and the second clause of verse 22, the majesty on God, answers to the first clause of verse 21. He prefers golden splendor to the rendering gold.
notes.limit: The north may be named because its wind clears the sky, but that is offered only as a perhaps. The word for golden splendor is the word for gold, and some translate it so, of gold found in the north.

cites.quote: Rather, "golden splendor." MAURER translates "gold." It is found in northern regions. ... the north--Brightness is chiefly associated with it (see on Job 23:9 ). Here, perhaps, because the north wind clears the air ( Pro 25:23 ). Thus this clause answers to the last of Job 37:21 ; as the second of this verse to the first of Job 37:21 . Inverted parallelism.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Morning stars and sons of God: one choir, twice
notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: the morning stars singing together answer to the sons of God shouting for joy. The sons of God are the angels, and the morning stars are read as the angels or as a picture of them, praising God as He laid the earth's foundations.

lines.words: while the morning stars sang together
and all the sons of God shouted for joy?

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes says angels are meant by the morning stars, as the phrase sons of God in the other half of the verse demands. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): the stars, said figuratively to sing, are symbols of the angels, and so they answer to the sons of God, the angels, in the parallel.

cites.quote: There can be little doubt that angelic beings are intended here ... That it refers to the angels, seems to be evident from the connection; and this interpretation is demanded in order to correspond with the phrase "sons of God" in the other member of the verse.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The stars are figuratively said to sing God's praises, as in Psa 19:1 ; Psa 148:3 . They are symbols of the angels, bearing the same relation to our earth, as angels do to us. Therefore they answer to "sons of God," or angels, in the parallel.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Boundaries, bars and doors: the sea's limits twice
notes.about: The second line says the first again. God fixed the sea's boundaries and set in place its bars and doors: both lines tell of the limits He set, which the sea may not pass, as the next verse says: “You may come this far, but no farther.”

lines.words: when I fixed its boundaries
and set in place its bars and doors,

original.note: In Hebrew the verb of the first line commonly means to break; here it is read of God measuring out the limits of the sea.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes says the sense the connection demands is that God measured out or set the limits of the sea, and that taking the line of God breaking up His fixed plans does not accord with the parallelism with the bars and doors. The Hebrew verb, he says, commonly means to break.

cites.quote: This is undoubtedly the sense which: the connection demands; and the idea in the common version, that God had broken up his fixed plans ... is not in accordance with the parallelism. The Hebrew word (שׁבר shâbar) indeed commonly means "to break, to break in pieces." ... The sense is, that God measured out or determined the limits of the sea.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Light and east wind: by what way do they spread?
notes.about: The second line asks of the east wind what the first asks of the light: by what way is it spread out over the earth? Light and wind stand together here, as things that come from one quarter and spread in courses no one can trace.

lines.words: In which direction is the lightning dispersed,
or the east wind scattered over the earth?

original.note: In Hebrew the first line's word is or, light, which the BSB gives as lightning; it can be read of light in general, such as the morning light spreading from one point over the whole earth.

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes reads the first line of the morning light spreading from one point, and holds that the parallelism demands a second line asking the same of the wind. Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch): light and wind stand together, alike untraceable in their courses. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) carries the question by what way into the second line, light and wind both coming from one quarter.

cites.quote: The reference here is to the light of the morning, that seems to come from one point, and to spread itself at once over the whole earth. ... the east wind, like the light, comes from a certain point, and seems to spread abroad over the world; and the question is, whether Job could explain this? This interpretation ... seems to be demanded by the parallelism

cites.quote: In Job 38:24 it is not, as in Job 38:19 , the place whence light issues, but the mode of the distribution of light over the earth, that is intended; as in Job 38:24 , the laws according to which the east wind flows forth, i.e., spreads over the earth. אור is not lightning ... but light in general: light and wind ... stand together as being alike untraceable in their courses.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: is . . . parted--parts, so as to diffuse itself over the whole earth, though seeming to come from one point. ... which scattereth--rather, "And by what way the east wind (personified) spreads (scattereth) itself." The light and east wind are associated together, as both come from one quarter, and often arise together

notes.short: A father for the rain, a mother for the ice
notes.about: Each verse asks its question twice. In verse 28 the father of the first line shows that the second asks who begets the dew. In verse 29 the womb of the first line shows that the second asks who bears the frost, as a mother does. Rain and dew have no created father, ice and frost no created mother.

lines.words: Does the rain have a father?
Who has begotten the drops of dew?
From whose womb does the ice emerge?
Who gives birth to the frost from heaven,

original.note: In Hebrew both verses use the one verb yalad. Beside a father it asks who begets; beside a womb it asks who bears, as a mother does.

notes.evidence: Franz Delitzsch (Keil and Delitzsch) says rain and dew have no created father, and ice and hoar-frost no created mother, and that the parallel lines in both verses show what the verb asks: in verse 28 after the one who begets, in verse 29 after the one who bears.

cites.quote: Rain and dew have no created father, ice and hoar-frost no created mother. The parallelism in both instances shows that מי הוליד asks after the one who begets, and מי ילדו the one who bears
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Traders barter for him, merchants share him out
notes.about: The second line says the first again: can men buy and sell him, or share him out among merchants? The merchants of the second line favour reading the first line as trade, as the BSB renders it, rather than as a feast made of him.

lines.words: Will traders barter for him
or divide him among the merchants?

original.note: In Hebrew the merchants are literally Canaanites, a people known as great traders.

notes.evidence: A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the parallel line rather supports reading the first as partners in trade who desire to buy him, and that the merchants are literally Canaanites, who were great merchants. Stanley Leathes (Ellicott's Commentary) renders the first line as bands of fishermen making traffic of him, which he says suits the parallelism better.
notes.limit: Older versions read the first line as companions making a banquet of him; some read it as men digging a pit for him.

cites.quote: make a banquet--The parallelism rather supports UMBREIT, "Do partners (in trade) desire to purchase him?" So the Hebrew ( Deu 2:6 ). merchants--literally, "Canaanites," who were great merchants
